notes.h: Trade vocabulary: visible and invisible trade
notes.b: Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services between countries. Exports leave a country and imports arrive in it, and data questions use these words constantly.
points: Visible trade is goods that can be seen and counted, such as cars, food and computer chips.
Invisible trade is services, which cannot be held or counted in the same way, such as software, financial services, tourism and aircraft leasing.
Balance of trade: the value of exports minus the value of imports, which gives one number that shows whether a country sells more than it buys.
A trade surplus means exports are greater than imports; a trade deficit means imports are greater than exports.
notes.tip: Data-response questions ask you to identify trade surpluses and deficits, so know which way round the subtraction goes: exports minus imports.

notes.b: The balance of trade is only part of the picture of a country's dealings with the world. The balance of payments is the wider record.
points: Balance of payments: the record of all money flows between a country and the rest of the world.
It includes trade in goods and services, plus investment flows (money put into businesses abroad), profits sent home, borrowing and transfers.
It is a wider measure than the balance of trade, which records only exports and imports, so the two are not the same thing.
notes.tip: Do not treat balance of trade and balance of payments as the same. Exams ask for both, and the balance of payments is the one that includes investment and profits.

notes.h: Effects of a trade deficit and of exports
notes.b: A country that keeps buying more from abroad than it sells pays a price at home, while exports bring benefits. Each effect follows from where the money goes.
points: A persistent trade deficit (imports greater than exports year after year) means money flows out of the country to pay for the extra imports.
The country may have to borrow or sell assets (things it owns, such as businesses or property) to pay for those imports.
Home industries and jobs can be lost as cheaper imports replace domestic production.
The currency (the country's money) may weaken when a country persistently imports more than it exports.
Exports bring jobs, tax revenue, foreign earnings and economic growth, because foreign buyers pay money into the country.
notes.tip: A question may ask for one disadvantage of a trade deficit or one advantage of exports for the Irish economy. Give one clear point with its reason, such as money flowing out, or jobs and tax revenue.

notes.b: A country that sells to many different countries is safer than one that sells mainly to one. This is the advantage of many export partners.
points: A country with many export partners is less dependent on any one market.
A recession (a fall in economic activity), tariff or crisis in one country, such as the US tariffs imposed in 2025, then does less damage to its overall trade, because the other markets keep buying.
notes.tip: To answer on one advantage of many export partners, say less dependence on one market, so trouble in one country does less damage.

notes.h: Free trade, protectionism and the WTO
notes.b: Governments can open their markets to imports or restrict them. Protectionism is the restricting approach, and international bodies try to set common rules.
points: Protectionism restricts imports to protect home industries from foreign competition, so home producers face less pressure from cheaper foreign goods.
Barriers to trade include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the quantity imported), subsidies (payments that help home producers compete with imports), and regulations.
Trade blocs (groups of countries that agree trade rules among themselves) remove barriers between their own members, so members trade with each other more easily than with outsiders.
GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) was signed in 1947 to reduce tariffs between countries, so goods cost less to trade.
The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was set up on 1 January 1995, with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland; it has over 160 member countries.
The WTO sets the rules of world trade and settles disputes between members, so countries have a common referee.
Fair trade gives producers in developing countries a guaranteed minimum price and a premium (an extra payment), shown by the Fairtrade mark.
notes.tip: The WTO dates from 1995 and GATT from 1947. Do not say the WTO was set up after the Second World War.

notes.b: World trade has grown much faster than world output since 1950, and most countries now depend on imports and exports. Several changes made this possible.
points: Falling trade barriers, through GATT and the WTO, made it cheaper to trade across borders.

Containerisation (shipping goods in standard-sized steel boxes) began with the first container ship voyage, the Ideal X of Malcolm McLean, USA, in 1956; containers made loading and shipping faster and cheaper.
Shanghai, China, has been the world's busiest container port since 2010.
Air freight and information and communication technology (ICT) speed up trade in high-value goods and services, for example by moving them quickly and sharing information instantly.
Multinational companies (MNCs, firms that operate in many countries) trade components between their own plants in different countries.
The entry of China and Eastern Europe into world trade added large new producers and markets, so there were more goods to sell and more buyers.
notes.tip: When asked why world trade has grown, give several drivers: falling barriers (GATT and the WTO), containerisation, air freight and ICT, MNCs, and the entry of China and Eastern Europe.

notes.b: The three triad areas and the rest of the world are linked by shipping routes and by products whose parts come from many countries. Because they are so linked, a disruption in one place spreads worldwide.
points: One product links many countries: the iPhone and Intel chip supply chains (the series of countries and firms that make a product's parts and assemble it) each pass through several countries. There is more on this in One multinational company (MNC).
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, and the Panama Canal, opened in 1914, are chokepoints (narrow passages that much shipping must use) on the shipping routes linking the triad.
In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for about six days, holding up hundreds of ships.
From late 2023 attacks on shipping in the Red Sea forced many ships to sail around the Cape of Good Hope, Africa.
The 2008-09 global financial crisis caused world trade to fall sharply in 2009.
COVID-19 (2020-21) disrupted supply chains, for example in the 2021 chip shortage.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to show the global nature of linkages. Use a named example, such as one product made in several countries, or a chokepoint such as the Suez Canal.

notes.b: Most of the world's trade and production is concentrated in three areas. The trading triad is North America, Europe and the Pacific Rim, the three core economic areas of the world.
points: The triad produces most of the world's manufactured goods, such as cars and electronics.
It holds the headquarters of most multinational companies (MNCs), so company decisions are made there.
Most world trade takes place among the three areas, and most foreign direct investment (money that firms invest in businesses and factories in other countries) flows between them.
notes.tip: No checked figure exists for each area's share of world trade, so do not quote a percentage. Describe the triad in words: goods, MNC headquarters, trade and investment.

notes.b: The USA is the triad's North American member and the dominant economy within it. Its trade is shaped by its size, its trade bloc and its use of tariffs.
points: The USA is the world's largest economy and its largest importer, so its demand matters to exporters everywhere.
It has had a trade deficit in goods every year since the mid-1970s, which means it imports more goods than it exports.
NAFTA (North American Free Trade Agreement: USA, Canada, Mexico) took effect on 1 January 1994.
USMCA (United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement) replaced NAFTA on 1 July 2020, so the three countries kept a trade bloc.
Mexico overtook China in 2023 as the largest source of US imports.
From 2018 the USA put tariffs (taxes on imports) on many Chinese goods in the US-China trade war.
In 2025 the USA raised tariffs on imports from most countries, which raised the price of goods entering the USA.
notes.tip: Do not take trade values or percentages from past-paper charts. Use the dated facts here: NAFTA then USMCA, the 2018 and 2025 tariff rounds, and Mexico in 2023.

notes.b: Europe is one of the three triad areas, and it trades as a bloc. The EU is a union of countries that trade freely with one another.
points: The EU is a single market (members trade as if in one market) of 27 member states, since the UK left the EU.
The single market began on 1 January 1993, removing barriers to trade between members, so goods move freely between them.
The EU is the largest trading bloc by value, with strong trade with the USA and China, for example in goods sold between the blocs.
The euro, the shared currency, was introduced in 1999; euro notes and coins followed in 2002.
In July 2025 the EU and USA agreed a 15% US tariff on most EU goods.

notes.b: In the triad, the Pacific Rim means mainly East and South-East Asia, together with Australia. India is not part of it.
points: Members include, for example, Japan, China, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the ASEAN countries and Australia.
ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) was founded in 1967 as a group of South-East Asian countries.
APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) was founded in 1989.
RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) has 15 Asia-Pacific members, including China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the ASEAN members.
RCEP was signed in November 2020 and came into force from 2022; its members hold about 30% of the world's population and GDP (the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year).
The Asian Tigers are South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore, fast-growing Asian economies. China and Japan are not Tigers.
notes.tip: Do not put India in the Pacific Rim. Remember that the Asian Tigers are South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore only.

notes.b: Japan is a Pacific Rim economy that grew after the Second World War by exporting manufactured goods. Its story shows how a country with few raw materials can grow by selling manufactured goods.
points: After the Second World War Japan's growth was based on exporting manufactured goods, mainly cars and electronics.
Japan has few raw materials, so it must import most of its oil, coal and iron ore.
Japan was the world's second-largest economy from the late 1960s until China overtook it in 2010; Germany overtook Japan in 2023.
Toyota, based in Toyota City, uses just-in-time production, which delivers parts as they are needed rather than storing them.
Other major Japanese companies are, for example, Honda, Sony and Nissan.

To avoid trade barriers, Japanese firms opened factories inside the EU and USA; Nissan's car plant at Sunderland, north-east England, opened in 1986, inside the European Economic Community (EEC, the EU's earlier name).
Japan's growth has been slower since the 1990s, so it is no longer expanding as quickly as it did after the war.
notes.tip: Cover Japan in this order: manufactured exports, few raw materials so it imports fuel and ores, Toyota's just-in-time production, factories inside the EU and USA, then slower growth since the 1990s.

notes.h: China: the workshop of the world
notes.b: China moved from a closed economy to the world's largest exporter of goods, which is why it is called the workshop of the world. Government reforms opened it to trade and investment.
points: Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms, from 1978, opened China's closed economy to foreign trade and investment.
The first Special Economic Zones (SEZs, areas with special rules to attract foreign firms) were set up in 1980, including Shenzhen beside Hong Kong.
Shenzhen is in mainland China and is not part of Hong Kong; it grew from a small town to over 17 million people (2020 census).
China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001, which gave it a place under world trade rules.
China has been the world's largest exporter of goods since 2009, and it overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
China runs a huge trade surplus, because it sells so much abroad; meaning its exports greatly exceed its imports.
The Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, links China to Asia, Africa and Europe through ports, railways and roads.
The trade war with the USA, begun in 2018, also affects China; the US side is in the North America notes.
notes.tip: Do not put Shenzhen in Hong Kong: it is in mainland China, beside Hong Kong. Do not call China an Asian Tiger either.

notes.h: South Korea: an export-led newly industrialised country (NIC)
notes.b: South Korea is the standard example of a newly industrialised country (NIC, a country that has recently built a large manufacturing economy). It went from poverty to high income by selling manufactured goods abroad.
points: South Korea was war-damaged by the Korean War (1950-53) and was one of the world's poorest countries in the early 1960s.
Under President Park Chung-hee (1961-79) it industrialised through exports and rose from poverty to high income.
Its economy is dominated by chaebol, family-controlled business groups such as Samsung (founded 1938), Hyundai, LG and SK.
Ulsan is home to Hyundai's shipyards, among the world's largest, and to a Hyundai car plant, as an example of an industrial city built on exports.
South Korea is a world leader in shipbuilding, cars, electronics and memory chips, and Samsung makes smartphones.
South Korea is one of the Asian Tigers and joined the OECD (the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) in 1996.
notes.tip: Structure South Korea as: war-damaged and poor, export-led industrialisation, the chaebol, then shipbuilding, cars, electronics and memory chips. It is an Asian Tiger.

notes.b: Not every region shares in the triad's trade. Some areas are left on the edges of world trade.
points: Africa, much of Latin America and South Asia hold only a small share of world trade, mostly in raw materials. There is more on this in How the global economy is organised.

notes.h: The international division of labour: the old pattern
notes.b: An international division of labour means that countries and regions specialise in different stages of production and different types of work. The first pattern grew out of colonial rule.
points: In the old, colonial pattern, colonies and developing countries exported raw materials and food, while Europe and later the USA manufactured goods and sold them back.
Sudan's Gezira Scheme, from 1925, grew irrigated cotton for the British (Lancashire) textile mills.
India exported raw cotton and tea to Britain under colonial rule, as an example of raw materials and food leaving a colony.
Ghana (then the Gold Coast) exported cocoa; Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana together grow over half of the world's cocoa today, still mostly exported unprocessed.
notes.tip: Use colonial trade here only as the old division of labour: raw materials and food out, manufactured goods back.

notes.h: The new international division of labour (from the 1960s-70s)
notes.b: From the 1960s-70s the pattern changed. Multinational companies began to split production, placing each stage where it suited them best.
points: Multinational companies moved assembly and routine manufacturing to newly industrialised countries (NICs) and low-wage countries.
The core (the rich, powerful economies) kept headquarters, research and development (R&D, work on new products and technology), design, finance and marketing.
The periphery (the poorer countries on the edge of the world economy) still supplies raw materials.
As an example, Apple's packaging carried the line 'Designed by Apple in California. Assembled in China.'

Intel's R&D is at Hillsboro, Oregon; its fabs (chip factories) include Leixlip in Ireland; assembly and test take place in Malaysia and Vietnam. There is more on this in One multinational company (MNC).
notes.tip: Use Apple's line, Designed by Apple in California and Assembled in China, or Intel's chain as your example of the new division of labour.

notes.h: The division of labour keeps changing
notes.b: The pattern is not fixed. Services are now divided between countries, and countries move up or spread to new places.
points: Services are now divided too: Bengaluru (Bangalore), India, is an IT services hub for firms such as Infosys, Wipro and Tata Consultancy Services, and IT and call centres are located in India.
China is moving into high-value products instead of only low-cost assembly.
Low-cost assembly is spreading to Vietnam, Bangladesh and India, because firms look for cheaper places to assemble.

notes.b: Ireland is a very open economy: its exports are larger than its GDP. It has moved from supplying food to the UK to hosting high-value manufacturing and services by multinational companies (MNCs).
points: Goods exports passed 200 billion euro in 2024 (CSO, the Central Statistics Office), a record.
Most of this export value is produced by MNC plants, not by Irish-owned firms, so large exports reflect MNC production.

Main goods exports: pharmaceuticals and chemicals (the largest category), medical devices (a cluster at Galway, with firms such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific), computer chips and electronics, and food and drink (beef, dairy and whiskey).
Main services exports: computer services (Ireland is one of the world's largest exporters of them), financial services, aircraft leasing and tourism.
Irish-based lessors (companies that own aircraft and lease them to airlines) manage over half of the world's leased commercial aircraft, from Dublin and Shannon.
Ireland has a large goods trade surplus, because it exports far more goods than it imports, the largest of it with the USA.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name two goods or two services that Ireland exports. Do not claim Irish-owned firms produce most exports, because MNC plants do.

notes.b: Where Irish goods go reflects who makes them. The main market is the USA.
points: The USA is the largest single market for Irish goods, taking about a third of them, which makes it Ireland's biggest buyer.
Other main markets, such as EU partners Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, then the UK and China.
US pharmaceutical and technology MNCs export from their Irish plants back to the USA and worldwide, which is why the USA dominates.
In early 2025 Irish exports to the USA rose sharply as US buyers stockpiled medicines (bought extra in advance) before new tariffs.
notes.tip: If asked for the main destination of Irish exports, answer the USA and give the reason: US MNCs export from their Irish plants. Do not quote export values from past-paper charts.

notes.h: Why exports to the UK changed
notes.b: Ireland's trade with the UK changed after the UK left the EU. Brexit is the usual reason to give.
points: The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020; the transition period (when the old trade rules still applied) ended on 31 December 2020.
Brexit brought customs checks (inspections of goods at the border) on trade with the UK and took the UK out of the EU single market.
A weaker pound makes Irish goods dearer for UK buyers.
Irish firms have diversified into other markets, so they depend less on the UK.
notes.tip: To explain why exports to the UK changed, give reasons such as customs checks, the UK leaving the single market, a weaker pound, and firms diversifying.

notes.b: Ireland's export success depends on a narrow base, which brings risk.
points: Ireland depends on a few US MNCs and on the US market, so a problem for those firms or that market hits Irish exports.
US tariffs from 2025 expose Irish exports to the USA to new barriers.
notes.tip: Name the two risks: dependence on a few US MNCs and the US market, and exposure to US tariffs from 2025.

notes.b: Data-response questions give charts and tables of trade and ask you to calculate. The method is the same every time.
points: Read values from the chart or table and state their units before calculating.
Balance of trade for one country: subtract imports from exports; a negative result is a trade deficit.
Difference between two countries: subtract the smaller value from the larger, so the answer is positive.
Total exports: add the values for every partner, so none is missed.
Use a bar chart to compare values between countries and a line graph to show change over time, because each suits that kind of data.
notes.tip: Data questions ask you to read values, calculate differences and totals, identify surpluses and deficits, name the country with the highest exports, and draw a suitable graph.

keyTerms.definition: The trade in physical goods that can be seen and counted, such as cars, food and computer chips.
The trade in services, such as software, financial services, tourism and aircraft leasing.
The value of a country's exports minus the value of its imports.
The record of all money flows between a country and the rest of the world, including trade, investment, profits, borrowing and transfers.
The situation in which the value of a country's imports is greater than the value of its exports.
Policies that restrict imports to protect home industries, using barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
A limit on the quantity of a product that can be imported.
The three core economic areas of North America, Europe and the Pacific Rim, which carry most world trade.
A country that has moved from low-income, mainly agricultural economies to manufacturing and exporting, such as South Korea.
A family-controlled business group in South Korea, such as Samsung, Hyundai, LG or SK.
The specialisation of countries and regions in different stages of production and different types of work.
Trade that guarantees producers in developing countries a minimum price and a premium, shown by the Fairtrade mark.

factCards.definition: Goods (over €200 billion in 2024, a record): pharmaceuticals and chemicals (largest), medical devices (Galway), chips and electronics, food and drink (beef, dairy, whiskey). Services: computer services, financial services, aircraft leasing, tourism.

factCards.definition: The USA takes about a third of Irish goods exports, then Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK and China. US pharmaceutical and technology MNCs export from Irish plants back to the USA. Risks: dependence on a few US firms and exposure to US tariffs (2025).

factCards.definition: Balance of trade = exports minus imports; a negative result is a deficit. Difference: subtract the smaller value from the larger. Total: add every partner's value. State units. Use a bar chart to compare countries and a line graph to show change over time.

questions.prompt: Examine how world trade is dominated by the USA, Europe and the Pacific Rim.
questions.model: The trading triad of North America, Europe and the Pacific Rim is the three core economic areas of the world. Together they produce most of the world's manufactured goods, hold the headquarters of most multinational companies, and carry most world trade among themselves, with most foreign direct investment flowing between them. The USA is the world's largest economy and largest importer, and it has run a trade deficit in goods every year since the mid-1970s. Its trade bloc, NAFTA, took effect on 1 January 1994 and was replaced by USMCA on 1 July 2020, and its trade is shaped by tariffs, including the trade war with China from 2018 and the wider tariffs of 2025. Mexico overtook China in 2023 as the largest source of US imports. The EU single market, created on 1 January 1993, now has 27 member states, and the euro came in 1999. It is the largest trading bloc by value and trades strongly with the USA and China, although the July 2025 agreement set a 15% US tariff on most EU goods. The Pacific Rim, mainly East and South-East Asia with Australia, includes Japan, which was the second-largest economy until China overtook it in 2010 and which exports cars and electronics while importing most of its oil, coal and iron ore. China has become the world's largest exporter of goods since 2009, with a huge trade surplus, after its reforms from 1978 and its WTO entry in 2001. South Korea, one of the Asian Tigers, grew from war-damaged poverty through export-led industrialisation under Park Chung-hee, and its chaebol such as Samsung and Hyundai dominate shipbuilding, cars, electronics and memory chips. Regional bodies such as ASEAN, APEC and RCEP (in force from 2022, with about 30% of world population and GDP) strengthen the Pacific Rim's position. Despite this, Africa, much of Latin America and South Asia hold only a small share of world trade, mostly in raw materials, so world trade is concentrated in the triad rather than shared across the world.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the new international division of labour, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: The international division of labour means that countries and regions specialise in different stages of production and different types of work. The old, colonial pattern had colonies and developing countries exporting raw materials and food, while Europe and later the USA manufactured goods and sold them back. Sudan's Gezira Scheme, from 1925, grew cotton for the Lancashire textile mills, India exported raw cotton and tea to Britain, and Ghana exported cocoa; Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire still grow over half of the world's cocoa, mostly exported unprocessed. The new international division of labour began in the 1960s and 1970s, when multinational companies moved assembly and routine manufacturing to newly industrialised countries (NICs) and low-wage countries. The core kept headquarters, research and development, design, finance and marketing, while the periphery still supplies raw materials. Apple's products show this clearly: the packaging said Designed by Apple in California and Assembled in China. Intel does its R&D in Hillsboro, Oregon, makes chips in fabs such as Leixlip in Ireland, and carries out assembly and test in Malaysia and Vietnam. South Korea shows how a country can move up the chain: from war-damaged and poor in the early 1960s, it industrialised through exports under Park Chung-hee and now leads in shipbuilding, cars, electronics and memory chips, with family-controlled chaebol such as Samsung and Hyundai. Services are now divided too: Bengaluru in India has become an IT services hub for firms such as Infosys, Wipro and Tata Consultancy Services, and call centres are also located in India. The pattern keeps changing: China is moving into high-value products, and low-cost assembly is spreading to Vietnam, Bangladesh and India. The new division therefore links all regions in one global production system, while the core still keeps the highest-value functions.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a trade surplus and a trade deficit, and give one disadvantage of a trade deficit.
questions.model: A trade surplus occurs when the value of a country's exports is greater than the value of its imports. A trade deficit occurs when the value of its imports is greater than the value of its exports. A disadvantage of a persistent trade deficit is that money flows out of the country to pay for the extra imports, so the country may have to borrow or sell assets to pay for them. Home industries and jobs can also be lost as cheaper imports replace domestic production.
